title: Joins
short: Choose joins by their actual cost
lead: Compare join algorithms using page I/O counts under the same data and buffer assumptions.
goals: Identify join semantics and the assumptions behind I/O calculations
Calculate the costs of tuple, page, and block nested-loop joins
Calculate index nested-loop join costs with clustering
Handle duplicates and combine the final merge pass with a sort-merge join

sections.title: Nested loops: change the unit of iteration
sections.html:
In a nested-loop join, the outer input drives the outer loop. The inner input is scanned again for each outer tuple, page, or block. Start with a block nested-loop join (BNLJ) example: R occupies 120 pages, S occupies 40 pages, and memory provides 12 buffer frames. Each frame holds one page.

  1. Choose R as the outer input and S as the inner input. Reserve 1 frame for reading S and 1 for collecting output, leaving 10 frames to hold a block of R.
  2. Read the first 10 pages of R into RAM. Keep them there while scanning all 40 pages of S to find every pair that satisfies the join condition.
  3. Replace them with the next 10 pages of R, then scan all of S again. R has 120/10=12 blocks, so repeat this process 12 times.

Reading R costs 120 page reads in total, with each page read once. Reading S costs 12×40=480 page reads. The total is 120+480=600 page I/Os. This model assumes that the inner input is rescanned for every outer block and that all of S is not retained between scans. It excludes CPU cost and writes of the final output.

Now express the calculation as a formula: M+ceil(M/(B−2))×N. Here M is the number of outer pages, N is the number of inner pages, and B is the number of buffer frames. B−2 frames hold the outer block, and ceil(M/(B−2)) counts the outer blocks. Round up because even an incomplete final block still requires an inner scan. The formula uses B≥3, and the inputs in this example are nonempty.

Key takeaway

Use the number of outer blocks to count inner scans. With 12 frames, the outer block uses 10 frames. Each outer block triggers one complete read of the inner input.

Reverse the roles: S as the outer input has 40/10=4 blocks, and each block scans all 120 pages of R. The cost is 40+ceil(40/10)×120=40+4×120=520 I/Os. If the outer input fits in B−2 frames, one block is enough and each input is read once. Calculate both outer choices because rounding can affect the result.

The two simpler variants use the same reasoning. Page nested loops holds one R page at a time and scans S 120 times: 120+120×40=4,920 I/Os, or M+MN in general. If R has 12,000 tuples, tuple nested loops scans S 12,000 times: 120+12,000×40=480,120 I/Os, or M+mN, where m is the number of outer tuples.

Related source material: PDF pages 4–11. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

sections.title: Index nested loops: find every match
sections.html:
An index nested-loop join reads an outer tuple, extracts its join key, and uses an index on the inner input to find every matching tuple. The cost of a lookup includes both finding the index entries and reading those inner tuples. A clustered index may place many matches on a small number of pages; an unclustered index may require many random I/Os. The index must support the join condition being used.

New worked example: after filtering, the outer input contains 25 tuples on 2 pages. Reading it costs 2 I/Os, and each unique-key lookup on the inner input costs 3 I/Os, including index access and the data fetch. There are 25 lookups, giving 2+25×3=77 I/Os. Counting 2+25 would require an additional assumption that reduces each lookup to 1 I/O.

In compact form, cost = M+m×C_lookup. M counts outer page reads, m counts outer tuples, and C_lookup is the I/O cost of finding all inner matches in one lookup. If costs vary by key, sum the individual lookups or use a suitable average. To isolate the effect of the probe count, hold the outer read cost at 2 I/Os and increase the number of probes to 2,500: the cost becomes 2+2,500×3=7,502 I/Os. This comparison deliberately holds the outer read cost fixed.

Key takeaway

A lookup must account for every match. An index does not automatically make a join cheap: cost also depends on the number of outer tuples, the number of matches, and the data pages that must be read.

Related source material: PDF pages 12–15. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

sections.title: Sort-merge and hashing: two ways to bring matches together
sections.html:
A sort-merge join sorts both inputs by the join key, then compares their current keys. Advance the pointer on the side with the smaller key. When the keys are equal, produce every pair across the two equal-key groups: 3 copies in R and 4 in S produce 3×4=12 tuples.

If the sorted results are written to disk, add the cost of sorting each input and then rereading the M pages of R and N pages of S for the merge: sort(R)+sort(S)+M+N. This scan formula assumes duplicate groups can be handled without additional reads; very large groups may increase the cost. The final merge pass of sorting can be combined with the join if enough buffers are available to read the runs from both inputs.

An in-memory hash join keeps a hash table for the smaller input in RAM during its build phase, then probes it with tuples from the larger input. When RAM is insufficient, Grace hash join uses the same hash function to divide R and S into corresponding partition pairs. R_i only needs to join S_i, where i is the partition number.

Count the operations: reading both inputs costs M+N; writing the partitions costs M+N; and rereading them for build and probe costs M+N. The total is 3(M+N), or 3×(120+40)=480 I/Os in this example. The formula excludes output writes and applies only when each build partition, including hash-table overhead, fits in RAM without further partitioning. Hash collisions still require checking key equality.

Related source material: PDF pages 16–41. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

Keep every pair when groups repeat or partitions skew

Merge join processes complete equal-key groups. Two R tuples r1,r2 with key 7 and three S tuples s1,s2,s3 with key 7 produce six pairs: (r1,s1), (r1,s2), (r1,s3), (r2,s1), (r2,s2), and (r2,s3). Advancing both inputs after one match loses valid pairs. Buffer and reuse a small group. When neither relevant group fits, spills or repeated reads may be needed. The simple M+N merge-scan cost therefore assumes suitable duplicate handling; the slide’s extreme nested-loop-style cost describes a rescan strategy, not every implementation.

An in-memory hash join retains all build tuples needed for matching, including duplicate-key tuples. Its hash table, metadata, and probe/output buffers must fit the actual memory budget. Only then can one read of each input give M+N input I/Os. The probe side can stream and need not fit in full.

Grace hash join applies a consistent partition function to both inputs and a suitable new hash distinction within a partition. Repartition an oversized build partition and its corresponding probe partition consistently; this adds I/O beyond 3(M+N). If one key creates an oversized group, rehashing cannot separate identical copies. A fallback can process chunks of one group against the other, with extra reads, preserving every pair. Unlike SUM or DISTINCT, an ordinary join cannot replace that group’s tuples with one aggregate state.

The teaching cost may exclude output to compare algorithms, but many-to-many results consume real CPU and output bandwidth. A×B matches for one key remain A×B output tuples for every correct join algorithm.

Original supplementary explanation and practice. Sources: Lecture 12 · physical PDF pp. 4, 17, 30, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 43; Lecture 11 · physical PDF pp. 22, 27.

sections.title: Exercise: choose under explicit assumptions
sections.html:
For R=120 pages, S=40 pages, and the 12 buffer frames above, compare the best BNLJ choice with Grace hash join. What changes if both inputs are already sorted and the output must follow the join-key order?

Show the solution

The lower BNLJ cost across the two orientations is 520 I/Os. Grace hash join costs 480 I/Os if each build partition fits in RAM and the distribution is suitable. With already-sorted inputs, a merge scan needs only 120+40=160 page reads and may preserve the required order, assuming duplicate groups cause no rereading. For a general inequality condition, the equijoin hash formula does not apply; nested loops remains applicable.

Related source material: PDF pages 31–43. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

Fuse the last sort pass only when its buffers fit

Let r and s be the remaining R and S run counts just before their final sorting merge. In the lecture’s basic fused model, allocate one page buffer per run and one for join output. Fusion needs r+s≤B−1, with duplicate groups handled without additional spill space or rescans. Enough memory for each separate two-pass sort does not automatically satisfy this combined requirement.

With R=120 pages, S=40 pages, and B=12, pass 0 creates ceil(120/12)=10 R-runs and ceil(40/12)=4 S-runs. Their 14 inputs exceed B−1=11, so the unchanged two-pass fused cost is inapplicable. Extra merging or a different memory allocation is needed. With B=16, the initial counts are 8 and 3; their total 11 fits in 15 input buffers under the stated duplicate assumptions.

For B=16, pass 0 reads and writes all 160 pages for 320 I/Os. The fused final pass reads them once for 160 more: 480 I/Os excluding join-output writes. Materialising both complete sorted files first costs 640 sorting I/Os, followed by 160 join reads: 800. Fusion saves 320 I/Os, one write and one read of both inputs.

If an input already supplies the required order, recalculate the run and cost accounting. Do not charge an unnecessary sort, and do not assume that sorted pages are cached.

Original supplementary explanation and practice. Sources: Lecture 12 · physical PDF pp. 16, 17, 30, 31, 32, 33.

quiz.question: Two groups with the same key contain 3 and 4 tuples. How many joined tuples do they produce?
quiz.explanation: A join retains every matching pair: 3×4=12. Each tuple in the first group matches every tuple in the second; the join does not automatically eliminate duplicate occurrences.
